newsitem.title: USA: Actor Charlie Sheen pleads no-contest to battery.
newsitem.headline: Actor Charlie Sheen pleads no-contest to battery.

text.p: Actor Charlie Sheen was given a one-year suspended prison sentence and put on probation for two years on Friday after pleading no-contest to a charge of battery for an attack on his girlfriend.

Judge Lawrence Mira also ordered the star of "Platoon", "Wall Street" and "Hot Shots" to pay $2,800 in fines and restitution, perform 300 hours of community service and attend eight counselling sessions.
In addition, Sheen was ordered to stay away from Brittany Ashland, who alleged the actor knocked her to the ground of his home during an argument last Dec. 20.

The woman, who Sheen's lawyer Donald Re asserted is an actress in pornographic films, has an outstanding civil suit against Sheen in which she is seeking damages for assault, battery, negligence, false imprisonment and emotional distress.
"You will not see me back in this courtroom," Sheen told the judge, who replied: "Not unless I order you."

In the criminal misdemeanor case in Malibu Municipal Court, Judge Mira had urged both parties to reach a settlement to avoid a trial. That resulted in Friday's agreement under which Sheen pleaded no-contest to a charge of battery with serious bodily injury.
Under California law, a plea of no-contest is the equivalent of a guilty plea but without the defendant actually admitting guilt.
Sheen, 31, the son of actor Martin Sheen and brother of Emilio Estevez, had been free on $20,000 bail since his arrest after the incident.

During Friday's court hearing, Ashland's attorney Gloria Allred asserted Sheen was drunk at the time of the attack and she submitted a photograph of Ashland with a cut lip that required seven stitches.
She said the actor pulled Ashland's hair so hard "she could feel her follicles crunch." But she quoted her client as saying: "I believe that Charlie is a good person who has some problems."
Sheen's lawyers told reporters they would have used a self-defence argument had the case gone to trial, but decided to plead no-contest to preserve the privacy of both parties.
